issues.legal_issue: A customary rule of lineal primogeniture does not continue to govern succession when the Hindu Succession Act makes provision for succession to the estate, unless the estate descends to a single heir under a covenant, agreement, or enactment.
material_facts: Succession to the ancestral estate had been governed by a customary rule of lineal primogeniture.

The estate’s asserted single-heir succession was not created by an enactment; Bengal Regulation 10 of 1800 recognized the continuance of local custom rather than itself making the estate descend to a single heir.
The estate holder died after the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
issues.conclusion: The customary rule of lineal primogeniture ceased to govern succession under section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act and was not saved by section 5(ii).
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act displaces a Hindu-law custom or usage concerning a matter for which the Act makes provision. Section 5(ii) is an exception for an estate that descends to a single heir by the terms of a covenant, agreement, or enactment; a regulation that merely preserves an existing custom does not itself bring the estate within that exception. Bengal Regulation 10 of 1800 was construed accordingly.

predicates.succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns who succeeds to an estate after its holder dies.
predicates.customary_single_heir_rule: Succession to the estate had been governed by a custom under which it passed to a single heir.
predicates.single_heir_descent_created_by_binding_i: The estate passed to a single heir under the terms of a covenant, agreement, or enactment rather than solely under custom.

issues.definition: When a succession dispute concerns an estate governed by a single-heir custom that was not itself created by a binding instrument, the customary rule no longer governs succession.

issues.legal_issue: When an intermediary held agricultural land in a representative capacity for coparceners, the statutory settlement of land in the intermediary’s possession extends to those coparceners as well.
material_facts: The estate vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act.
The family remained joint, and no partition between the relevant family members had occurred.
The court held that land possessed by the estate holder on behalf of other coparceners would be deemed settled with all of them.
issues.conclusion: If the estate holder possessed the land in a representative capacity for the coparceners, the land was deemed settled with them all, and they became raiyats; the holder’s death did not make the land the exclusive property of his heirs.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act deems qualifying land in an intermediary’s khas possession to be settled with that intermediary. Where the intermediary possessed the land representatively for coparceners, the court held that the statutory settlement extends to all those on whose behalf the land was possessed.

predicates.land_reform_vesting_dispute: The proceeding concerns the effect of land vesting in the State under a land-reform scheme.
predicates.agricultural_land_in_intermediary_posses: The land was used for agriculture and was in the intermediary’s possession when the estate vested.
predicates.representative_possession_for_coparcener: The intermediary held the land on behalf of other members of the joint family rather than solely for himself.

issues.definition: In a land-reform vesting dispute, agricultural land held by an intermediary for coparceners is settled with those coparceners as well as with the intermediary.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory restriction on alienation after restoration of property under the encumbered-estates law applies only when the specified restoration conditions are established.
material_facts: The estate had previously been protected under the Chota Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act and was later released from its operation.
The plaintiff argued that a maintenance grant was void for want of the Commissioner’s sanction under section 12A.
The plaintiff did not establish that possession and enjoyment had been restored in the circumstances specified in the relevant clauses of section 12.
issues.conclusion: Section 12A did not establish that the grant was void because the plaintiff failed to prove the conditions that attracted the restriction.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 12A of the Chota Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act, 1876, the restriction on alienation without the Commissioner’s previous sanction applies only when possession and enjoyment are restored in the circumstances specified in the first or third clause of section 12. The party asserting the restriction bears the burden of establishing those conditions.

predicates.challenge_to_alienation_under_estates_la: A party challenges an alienation as invalid under a law governing estates under statutory management.
predicates.property_previously_under_statutory_mana: The property had been subject to the statutory management regime addressed by that law.
predicates.qualifying_restoration_conditions_proven: The party challenging the alienation proved that possession and enjoyment were restored in circumstances that trigger the statutory restriction.

issues.definition: Where a challenge to an alienation concerns previously managed property but the required restoration circumstances are not proved, the statutory restriction is not established.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered document requiring registration may be used to establish a collateral matter, including the nature of a person’s possession, but not as evidence of the transaction affecting the property.
material_facts: The maintenance deed was unstamped and unregistered, although it required registration.
The deed could not be received as evidence of a transaction affecting the land.
The nature of the defendant’s possession was a collateral matter for which the deed was relied on.
issues.conclusion: The maintenance deed could be considered for the collateral purpose of ascertaining the nature of the defendant’s possession.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 49 of the Indian Registration Act require registration of specified documents and restrict the use of an unregistered document as evidence of a transaction affecting immovable property. The proviso to section 49 permits its use as evidence of a collateral transaction or purpose that does not itself require a registered instrument.

rule.if: registration_evidence_dispute and document_requires_registration and document_unregistered and collateral_possession_purpose

predicates.registration_evidence_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a document may be used as evidence about possession of property.
predicates.document_requires_registration: The document is of a kind that the law requires to be registered.
predicates.collateral_possession_purpose: The document is offered to establish the nature of possession rather than to prove the transaction affecting the property.

issues.definition: An unregistered document requiring registration may be used in a registration-evidence dispute to establish the collateral nature of possession, but not to prove the property transaction itself.

issues.legal_issue: A family member’s possession under a maintenance grant from the holder of an impartible estate is not trespass merely because the grant document is invalid or unregistered.
material_facts: The defendant was a member of the joint Hindu family and was entitled to maintenance from the holder of the impartible estate.
The estate holder had given the defendant the disputed land under a maintenance grant and executed a maintenance deed.
The deed’s formal validity was disputed, but its execution was not denied.
issues.conclusion: The defendant’s possession could not be treated as that of a trespasser, and the High Court erred in treating it as such.
issues.legal_principle: A member of a joint Hindu family is entitled to maintenance from the holder of an impartible estate. Where the holder has put that member in possession under a maintenance grant, the possession is not that of a trespasser merely because the deed is invalid for want of registration or stamping; the deed may be considered collaterally to ascertain the nature of possession.

predicates.possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a person in possession of family property may be treated as a trespasser.
predicates.family_member_entitled_to_maintenance: The person in possession was a member of the family entitled to maintenance from the estate holder.
predicates.estate_holder_granted_possession_for_mai: The estate holder put the family member in possession of the disputed property as maintenance.

issues.definition: A family member entitled to maintenance who was put in possession for that purpose does not possess as a trespasser merely because the grant document is formally invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An ancestral estate that is impartible by custom remains joint family property for the purpose of survivorship unless the right to succeed to it has been renounced or surrendered.
material_facts: The court found that the estate was ancestral and impartible by custom.
The family’s joint status continued, and no partition had occurred.
The record did not establish that the junior family members had renounced or surrendered their right to succeed to the estate.
The estate holder died after the Hindu Succession Act came into force, and the court rejected the contention that the estate was exclusively his property for succession purposes.
issues.conclusion: The estate remained joint family property for the purpose of survivorship, although it was impartible and the customary rule of primogeniture no longer governed succession under the Hindu Succession Act.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Mirza Raja Shri Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Raj Manne Sultan Bahadur v. Shri Pushavathi Visweswar Gajapathi Raj, which relied on Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi: an ancestral estate impartible by custom is not the holder’s separate property, and the right of survivorship remains an incident of joint family ownership. Chinnathayal alias Veeralakshmi v. Kulasekara Pandiya Naicker requires proof of an express or implied intention to renounce or surrender the right to succeed before the estate can be treated as separate for succession. The court also recognized that a holder may alienate an impartible estate by gift or will unless restricted by family custom or tenure. Sections 4 and 6 of the Hindu Succession Act govern the displacement of custom and statutory devolution, respectively.

rule.if: succession_in_impartible_estate and ancestral_estate and customary_impartibility and joint_family_status_continued and not succession_right_renounced

predicates.succession_in_impartible_estate: The proceeding concerns succession to an estate that is asserted to be impartible.
predicates.ancestral_estate: The estate came to its holder as ancestral family property.
predicates.customary_impartibility: A custom made the estate impartible.
predicates.joint_family_status_continued: The family remained joint, with no partition ending that status.
predicates.succession_right_renounced: The junior family members expressly or impliedly renounced or surrendered their right to succeed to the estate.

issues.definition: An ancestral estate that is impartible by custom remains joint family property for survivorship when the family remains joint and its members have not renounced their succession right.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer in possession of joint property cannot be ousted through a suit for possession of selected property and mesne profits; the proper remedy is a partition suit in which the parties’ equities can be adjusted.
material_facts: The defendant was a co-sharer in the joint family property and was in possession of the disputed land.
The plaintiff sought possession of plots in one village and mesne profits rather than partition of the joint properties.
The High Court granted joint possession and mesne profits, but the Supreme Court set that decree aside.
issues.conclusion: The proper remedy was a regular suit for partition, not a suit for possession of the selected plots and mesne profits; the High Court’s decree was set aside and the trial court’s decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: A co-sharer may remain in possession of joint property. Where possession is held in that capacity, the appropriate remedy is partition, at which the equities of the parties can be adjusted, rather than an action seeking possession of selected parts of the property and mesne profits.

predicates.co_sharer_possession_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking possession of property from a person alleged to be a co-sharer.
predicates.defendant_is_co_sharer_in_joint_property: The person in possession has the status of a co-sharer in the joint property.
predicates.claim_seeks_selected_property_possession: The claimant seeks possession of selected parts of the property or mesne profits instead of partition of the joint property.

issues.definition: When a co-sharer possesses joint property and the claim seeks selected-property possession or mesne profits, partition is the proper remedy.
